title: Some definite service (Newman)
hook: God has created me to do him some definite service
tomorrow: a ship stuck at sea, no wind, a dark night. what did Newman ask for?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales's letters: faults matter, and so does beginning again without shock. The line was have patience with yourself.

Run a necklace chain, or a bike chain, through your fingers. Every link is the same small loop, nothing special on its own. Take one out, and the whole thing stops working. John Henry Newman, an English priest who later became a cardinal, used that picture for a human life. In a page from his Meditations and Devotions he also wrote something that reads like a job offer with the job description left blank on purpose.
screen: `A CHAIN IN YOUR FINGERS.` → `ONE LINK MISSING.` → `A JOB OFFER, LEFT BLANK.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Newman writes: "God has created me to do Him some definite service; He has committed some work to me which He has not committed to another." Not service in general. A definite piece, handed to one person and not shared out. Second, the blank. "I have my mission—I may never know it in this life, but I shall be told it in the next." He doesn't promise a clear sense of purpose by a certain age. He promises a purpose, and leaves the seeing for later. Third, the size. He calls himself "a link in a chain", a bond between people. The work may be small and hidden, a connection rather than a monument. Fourth, the surprise, and it's the line to tell a friend tonight: "If I am in sickness, my sickness may serve Him; in perplexity, my perplexity may serve Him; if I am in sorrow, my sorrow may serve Him." So the service isn't only what gets done on good days. A sick bed can be part of it. Confusion can be part of it. That's why the passage ends with Newman trusting that, wherever he is, he can never be thrown away.
screen: `A WORK NOT GIVEN TO ANOTHER.` · `I MAY NEVER KNOW IT HERE.` · `A LINK IN A CHAIN.` · `EVEN SICKNESS MAY SERVE.` · then, large: `A DEFINITE SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Hook the fingers of your two hands together, like two links in a chain, and feel the gentle pull both ways. With each breath, let one person come to mind whom your life quietly holds on to. If you pray, you can ask Newman's question with them: what is mine to do?
Some definite service. Newman's phrase for the work God gives each person, given to no one else, known or not. Today's word.
Pocket this one: a definite service, a link you already are, not a job you have to hunt for. Until next time.

howItsDone: Some Catholics keep Newman's meditation on some definite service as a prayer to reread in times of doubt, especially when the way ahead is unclear.

fork.setup: your friend has the flu the week of his big game and texts that he's useless to everyone. what would Newman's meditation say?
options: his sickness may serve too; he can't be thrown away.
service starts again once he's healthy and back on the field.
service is for the strong; he should rest and stop worrying.
fork.reveal: Newman writes that sickness, perplexity and sorrow may all serve God, which is why he trusts he can never be thrown away.

options: Newman says the same: a work given only to you, which you may not know until later.
He will. Newman says you'll see your purpose clearly once you've graduated.
It's soccer, obviously. Newman says your purpose is whatever you're best at.
chat.meaning: Newman writes that God committed some work to him and not to another, and that he may never know it in this life.
